focus_areas.opener: You hit 3× background task throughput at InCruiter with a Redis-powered queue — what was the core bottleneck you were solving before that system existed?

dimensions.label: Redis queue design — retries and deduplication
dimensions.resume_anchor: Built a Redis-powered distributed queue system enabling asynchronous job processing with retries, deduplication, and worker scaling, increasing background task throughput by 3×.
dimensions.surface: In your Redis queue at InCruiter, how did you represent a job that needed to be retried — what did the data structure in Redis actually look like?
dimensions.mechanism: Deduplication in a distributed queue means the same job can arrive twice simultaneously from two workers — how did your implementation prevent both from executing?
dimensions.boundary: A job in your queue fails on attempt 2 of 3, but the worker process dies mid-retry before updating Redis — what state is that job in, and how does your system recover it?

dimensions.label: Multi-tenant isolation and granular RBAC
dimensions.resume_anchor: Architected and delivered a multi-tenant backend supporting secure tenant isolation, per-client configurations, and granular RBAC controls for enterprise clients.
dimensions.surface: In the multi-tenant backend at InCruiter, at what layer did tenant isolation actually get enforced — the database query, the middleware, or somewhere else?
dimensions.mechanism: Granular RBAC means permissions exist below the role level — how did your data model distinguish between a permission attached to a role versus one assigned directly to a user within a tenant?
dimensions.boundary: Two enterprise tenants share the same underlying database — give me the specific scenario where a misconfigured query could leak one tenant's data to another, and what your architecture does to prevent it.

dimensions.label: 30% API latency reduction — query optimization and caching
dimensions.resume_anchor: Engineered scalable RESTful microservices using Node.js/Express for authentication, user management, and candidate workflows, reducing API latency by 30% through optimized queries and caching.

coverage_map.application_question: Imagine your PM comes to you tomorrow and says: 'We're launching a B2B version of Gadgets-Of-Galaxy where companies can have multiple employees sharing one company account — each employee logs in individually but all purchases bill to the company. The JWT auth system you built for login and signup needs to support this.' How would you approach redesigning the authentication and authorization layer to handle this multi-tenant, role-within-organization model?
coverage_map.implementation_anchor: I implemented JWT-based authentication for login and signup with protected routes and token verification on the backend using Node.js and Express.js.

dimensions.label: JWT Payload Structure
dimensions.description: Tests whether the candidate understands that the existing JWT payload (likely just userId, email, role) needs to be extended to carry organization/tenant context without bloating the token or creating security leaks between tenants
expected_approaches: Add orgId and orgRole fields to the JWT payload at login time
Issue a separate org-scoped token after a user selects their active organization
Keep JWT minimal and resolve org membership server-side on each request using the userId
dimensions.surfacing_question: Your current tokens probably store something like a user ID and maybe a role — what changes when the same user needs to act on behalf of a company, and how does the token reflect that?

dimensions.label: Role-Based Access Within Org
dimensions.description: Tests whether the candidate can differentiate authentication (who you are) from authorization (what you can do within an org), and design permission levels like company admin vs. regular employee
expected_approaches: Define org-level roles (admin, member, viewer) stored in a join table linking users to organizations
Use middleware on protected routes that checks both the JWT validity AND the user's role within the org fetched from DB
Embed permissions array in JWT payload for fast route-level checks
dimensions.surfacing_question: If a company admin should be able to see all employee orders but a regular employee can only see their own — where in your current Express.js setup does that check actually happen?

dimensions.label: Tenant Data Isolation
dimensions.description: Tests awareness that without scoping database queries to an organization, a user from Company A could potentially access Company B's data — a critical security boundary for B2B
expected_approaches: Always filter queries by orgId extracted from the verified JWT or session
Add orgId as a foreign key to all relevant tables (orders, carts, invoices) and enforce it in every query
Use database row-level security policies to enforce tenant boundaries at the DB layer
dimensions.surfacing_question: Once multiple companies are in the same database, what stops an authenticated employee of Company A from accidentally — or intentionally — seeing Company B's purchase history?

dimensions.label: Backward Compatibility of Protected Routes
dimensions.description: Tests whether the candidate thinks about how their existing token verification middleware on protected routes would need to change — and whether individual consumer accounts can coexist with B2B org accounts
expected_approaches: Add an optional orgId check in middleware — if present, apply org-scoped logic; if absent, fall back to individual user logic
Version the API routes (/v1 vs /v2) so B2B routes are separate from existing consumer routes
Introduce a user 'account type' flag in the token to branch logic at the middleware level
dimensions.surfacing_question: Your current protected routes work for individual shoppers right now — what breaks or needs to change in that middleware when a request comes from a B2B employee token?

dimensions.label: User-to-Org Onboarding
dimensions.description: Tests product thinking and basic security awareness around how employees join a company account — this is a new flow that doesn't exist in the original single-user auth system
expected_approaches: Admin sends an invite link with a short-lived signed token; new user registers and gets linked to the org on acceptance
Admin manually adds employee emails; on their next login the system detects and prompts org association
Organization code or domain-based auto-join (e.g., all @company.com emails auto-join that org)
dimensions.surfacing_question: If a company admin wants to add a new employee to their account, what does that flow look like from the moment the admin clicks 'invite' to the moment the employee can start placing orders?
